    Quant reference

    GMAT Formula + Trigger Cheat Sheet

    See the wording, identify the hidden structure, then use the formula
    19 sections

    1. Percentages

    Triggers: “A is what percent of B?”, “of”, “increased/decreased by p%”.

    Percent = Part ÷ Whole × 100p% of x = (p ÷ 100) × xPercent change = (New − Original) ÷ Original × 100

    Always divide percent change by the original.

    Increase: New = Original(1 + p)   |   Decrease: New = Original(1 − p)

    Reverse: after +20% use ×5/6; after −20% use ×5/4; after +25% use ×4/5; after −25% use ×4/3.

    Successive changes: Final = Original(1 + p₁)(1 + p₂)

    Multiply factors; do not add percentages. 1.25 × 0.8 = 1.

    2. Ratios

    Triggers: group comparison, parts, subgroup total, or one side staying unchanged.

    A:B = 3:5 → A = 3k, B = 5k, total = 8k5 parts = 60 → 1 part = 12

    For A:B = 3:5 and total 64: 8k = 64, so A = 24 and B = 40.

    When one group is unchanged, scale both ratios until that side matches, then compare the changing side.

    3. Fractions

    Triggers: “of” means multiply; “remaining” means remaining ÷ whole.

    a/b + c/d = (ad + bc) ÷ bda/b × c/d = ac ÷ bd

    Cancel before multiplying whenever possible.

    a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c

    Keep–Change–Flip.

    Fraction remaining = Remaining ÷ Whole

    4. Algebra Word Translation

    Trigger: relational wording that must become an equation before calculation.

    “35 less than 3x” = 3x − 35“12 greater than twice x” = 2x + 12“Twice x less 12” = 2x − 12

    Multi-step pattern

    1. Define x.
    2. Translate the first relationship.
    3. Use a total.
    4. Apply a ratio.
    5. Use another total.
    6. Find the leftover.

    5. Distance, Rate & Time

    Triggers: travel, speed, meeting, chasing, head start, or average speed.

    D = RT   |   R = D/T   |   T = D/RToward each other: relative speed = R₁ + R₂Same direction: relative speed = Rfast − Rslow

    Head start: calculate the early distance, subtract it from the gap, then use relative speed.

    Average speed = Total distance ÷ Total time

    Do not average speeds unless equal time was spent at each speed.

    6. Work Rates

    Triggers: “finishes one job in t hours”, “working together”, or equal-time job percentages.

    One job in t hours → Rate = 1/tTogether: Rtogether = R₁ + R₂Work = Rate × Time   |   Remaining = 1 − Completed

    “Takes 3/4 as much time” → time ratio 3:4 → rate ratio 4:3.

    For equal time, work is proportional to rate: 40%:60% = 2:3.

    Rates 4:3 → R₁ = 4k, R₂ = 3k, together = 7k

    7. Quantity × Rate = Total

    Trigger: number of units/workers/employees combined with output, price, or salary per unit.

    Total = Quantity × Rate
    • Revenue = Units × Price per unit
    • Output = Workers × Output per worker
    • Distance = Time × Speed
    • Work = Time × Work rate
    • Payroll = Employees × Salary per employee
    30% fewer × 20% more each → 0.70 × 1.20 = 0.84

    8. Averages

    Trigger: “average” → think total ÷ count.

    Average = Total ÷ Number of itemsTotal = Average × Number of itemsNumber of items = Total ÷ Average

    9. Weighted Averages

    Trigger: different groups or percentages contribute to one overall average.

    Weighted avg = [(n₁a₁) + (n₂a₂)] ÷ (n₁ + n₂)n₁a₁ + n₂a₂ = total count × overall average

    Example: 10(28) + 16x = (10 + x)(20).

    Percentage weights: Average = w₁v₁ + w₂v₂

    Example: 0.8(5) + 0.2(10) = 6.

    10. Direct Proportionality

    Trigger: “directly proportional”.

    y ∝ x → y = kx

    If x doubles, y doubles; if x triples, y triples.

    Write the equation with k immediately.

    11. Inverse Proportionality

    Trigger: “inversely proportional”.

    y ∝ 1/x → y = k/x

    If x doubles, y halves.

    12. Simultaneous vs Chain Proportionality

    “Directly proportional to both x and z” means both variables act at the same time.

    y ∝ xz → y = kxz

    Chain: R ∝ M and M ∝ P.

    R = k₁M, M = k₂P → R = KP

    A chain gives R ∝ P. Do not automatically write R = kMP.

    13. Proportionality in DS

    Trigger: a DS statement supplies a direct, inverse, or simultaneous proportionality.

    Q ∝ MH → Q = kMH

    Ask whether the statement determines the needed constant k. It may be sufficient even without calculating the requested final value.

    In a chain, one statement may determine k₁ and another k₂; both can be required.

    14. Data Sufficiency Rules

    1. Test statement (1) alone.
    2. Test statement (2) alone.
    3. Combine only if both alone are insufficient.

    Yes/No: always Yes or always No is sufficient.

    Prove insufficiency: find two valid cases with different answers.

    Boundary traps: greater than, less than, at least, at most, exactly. “At most 90” means x ≤ 90; “at least 20%” means x ≥ 20%.

    15. Prime Factors, Factors, GCF & LCM

    Triggers: exact factor count, integer dimensions, equal groups, or repeating cycles.

    72 = 2³ × 3²

    Prime factorization is multiplication, not addition.

    n = pᵃqᵇrᶜ → positive factors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)

    Each exponent gives the available powers from 0 through that exponent; multiply the choices.

    36 factor pairs: 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6

    List pairs only to √N. For a perfect square, the middle pair appears once; do not blindly divide the factor count by 2.

    Greatest equal groups, no leftovers → GCF. First time cycles meet / smallest divisible by both → LCM.

    Divisible by a and b → divisible by LCM(a,b)

    16. Divisibility, Remainders, Parity & Signs

    Trigger: “remainder r when divided by d” → write the algebraic form first.

    n = dk + r, where 0 ≤ r < d

    Example: n = 7k + 4, so n + 3 reaches the next multiple of 7. If n = 7k + 3, then 5n + 4 leaves remainder 5 upon division by 7.

    2: last digit even · 3/9: digit sum · 4: last 2 digits · 8: last 3 digits · 5: 0 or 5 · 6: both 2 and 3 · 10: 0

    If 18 divides n, then 2, 3, 6 and 9 also divide n.

    odd+odd=even · odd+even=odd · even+even=evenProduct odd → every factor odd · even × anything → evenEven number of negative factors → positive · odd number → negative

    17. Perfect Powers, Consecutive Integers & Units Digits

    Perfect square → every prime exponent evenPerfect cube → every prime exponent is a multiple of 3

    Consecutive: n, n+1, n+2. Consecutive odd/even: n, n+2, n+4.

    For three consecutive integers, the middle number is the average. Sum 72 → middle 24 → 23, 24, 25.

    Huge power + units digit → use the final digit’s cycle, never calculate the full power.

    0→0 · 1→1 · 2→2,4,8,6 · 3→3,9,7,1 · 4→4,6 · 5→5 · 6→6 · 7→7,9,3,1 · 8→8,4,2,6 · 9→9,1
    1. Keep only the base’s units digit.
    2. Identify the cycle length.
    3. Use exponent mod cycle length.
    4. Remainder 0 means the final cycle position.
    7¹⁰³: 103 mod 4 = 3 → units digit 3

    18. Absolute Value, Inequalities & Exponents

    |x| = a → x = a or x = −a|x − 3| = 5 → x − 3 = ±5 → x = 8 or −2

    Endpoints: < or > excludes; ≤ or ≥ includes.

    3 < x < 8, integer x → 4, 5, 6, 7aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ · aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ · a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0 · √(a²) = |a|

    Example: 2ˣ × 2ˣ⁺³ = 2¹⁵ → 2x + 3 = 15 → x = 6.

    19. GMAT Trigger Wording

    Arithmetic is often disguised. Constraint wording is part of Quant skill, not merely reading comprehension. Once a rule is understood, move to a disguised application.

    “of”
    Multiply
    “A is what percent of B?”
    A ÷ B × 100
    “increased/decreased by p%”
    Multiply by (1+p) or (1−p)
    “takes 3/4 as much time”
    Time 3:4 → rate 4:3
    “X% of the job in the same time as Y%”
    Rate ratio X:Y
    “finishes one job in t hours”
    Rate = 1/t
    “working together”
    Add rates
    “average”
    Total ÷ count
    “groups contribute to one average”
    Weighted average
    “workers × output per worker”
    Quantity × rate = total
    “directly proportional”
    y = kx
    “inversely proportional”
    y = k/x
    “directly proportional to both x and z”
    y = kxz
    R ∝ M and M ∝ P
    Chain → R ∝ P
    “exactly N positive factors”
    Prime factors + exponent-count formula
    “integer dimensions / fixed area”
    Factor pairs
    “greatest possible equal groups”
    GCF
    “smallest divisible by both / first time together”
    LCM
    “remainder r when divided by d”
    n = dk + r
    “product is odd”
    Every factor is odd
    “product is negative”
    Odd number of negative factors
    “perfect square / cube”
    Prime exponents even / multiples of 3
    “consecutive odd/even integers”
    n, n+2, n+4
    “huge power + units digit”
    Units-digit cycle
    “|expression| = a”
    Expression = +a or −a
    “a < x < b”
    Endpoints excluded
    “same base multiplied / divided”
    Add / subtract exponents
    “power raised to a power”
    Multiply exponents
